papers.title: Functional connectomics reveals general wiring rule in mouse visual cortex
papers.citation: NeuroTrailblazers Consortium (2021). Functional connectomics reveals general wiring rule in mouse visual cortex. Nature. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-08840-3
papers.abstract: ; however, broader connectivity rules remain unknown. Here we leverage the millimetre-scale MICrONS dataset to analyse synaptic connectivity and functional properties of neurons across cortical layers and areas. Our results reveal that neurons with similar response properties are preferentially connected within and across layers and areas-including feedback connections-supporting the universality of 'like-to-like' connectivity across the visual hierarchy. Using a validated digital twin model, we separated neuronal tuning into feature (what neurons respond to) and spatial (receptive field location) components. We found that only the feature component predicts fine-scale synaptic connections beyond what could be explained by the proximity of axons and dendrites. We also discovered a higher-order rule whereby postsynaptic neuron cohorts downstream of presynaptic cells show greater functional similarity than predicted by a pairwise like-to-like rule. Recurrent neural networks trained on a simple classification task develop connectivity patterns that mirror both pairwise and higher-order rules, with magnitudes similar to those in MICrONS data. Ablation studies in these recurrent neural networks reveal that disrupting like-to-like connections impairs performance more than disrupting random connections. These findings suggest that these connectivity principles may have a functional role in sensory processing and learning, highlighting shared principles between biological and artificial systems.

ocar.opportunity: In mouse V1, excitatory neurons with similar responses are more likely to connect, but whether that like-to-like rule holds across layers, areas, and feedback, and whether it is more than axon–dendrite proximity, was open at millimeter scale.
ocar.challenge: Separating feature tuning from receptive-field location, and asking about higher-order structure among a cell’s postsynaptic cohort, requires jointly measured function and synapses across a large volume.
ocar.action: In Nature (2025), Ding, Fahey, Papadopoulos, Tolias, Reimer and the MICrONS consortium analyze synaptic connectivity and visual responses in the millimeter-scale MICrONS mouse visual-cortex dataset, using a validated digital-twin model to split feature versus spatial tuning, then train recurrent nets on a classification task and ablate like-to-like weights.
ocar.resolution: Like-to-like connectivity appears within and across layers and areas, including feedback, and only the feature component of tuning predicts fine-scale synapses beyond geometric proximity. Postsynaptic cohorts are more functionally similar than pairwise like-to-like predicts. RNNs develop similar pairwise and higher-order patterns, and ablating like-to-like connections hurts task performance more than ablating random ones.
ocar.future_work: They suggest these rules may matter for sensory processing and learning in both biological and artificial systems; whether they hold outside visual cortex is not shown here.

papers.plain_language_summary: Brain cells that like the same pictures tend to wire to each other, not just next door but across visual areas. This mouse study finds that pattern in a cubic-millimeter wiring-and-activity map, and a simple artificial network grows the same habit when trained to classify.

summaries.beginner: Brain cells that like the same pictures tend to wire to each other, not just next door but across visual areas. This mouse study finds that pattern in a cubic-millimeter wiring-and-activity map, and a simple artificial network grows the same habit when trained to classify.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature (2025), Ding, Fahey, Papadopoulos and colleagues use the MICrONS millimeter-scale mouse visual cortex dataset. Neurons with similar response properties connect preferentially within and across layers and areas, including feedback, supporting a general like-to-like rule in the visual hierarchy. A digital twin decomposes tuning into feature and spatial parts; only feature similarity predicts fine-scale synapses beyond axon–dendrite proximity. A higher-order rule is that postsynaptic cohorts of a given presynaptic cell are more similar than pairwise statistics predict. RNNs trained on classification spontaneously acquire both rules; targeted ablation of like-to-like weights impairs performance more than random ablation.
summaries.advanced: Functional analyses use MICrONS plus additional two-photon experiments in ten mice (3 female, 7 male, 78–190 days) of Slc17a7-Cre;Ai162 background; MICrONS itself is from one 75-day-old male of the same strain. Sex-disaggregated analysis was not performed because of sample size. “Magnitudes similar” to MICrONS in RNNs is the authors’ comparison. Like-to-like is reported for the excitatory/visual-hierarchy setting they analyze, not all cell classes.

papers.title: A presynaptic source drives differing levels of surround suppression in two mouse retinal ganglion cell types
papers.citation: NeuroTrailblazers Consortium (2024). A presynaptic source drives differing levels of surround suppression in two mouse retinal ganglion cell types. bioRxiv. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-44851-w
papers.abstract: In early sensory systems, cell-type diversity generally increases from the periphery into the brain, resulting in a greater heterogeneity of responses to the same stimuli. Surround suppression is a canonical visual computation that begins within the retina and is found at varying levels across retinal ganglion cell types. Our results show that heterogeneity in the level of surround suppression occurs subcellularly at bipolar cell synapses. Using single-cell electrophysiology and serial block-face scanning electron microscopy, we show that two retinal ganglion cell types exhibit very different levels of surround suppression even though they receive input from the same bipolar cell types. This divergence of the bipolar cell signal occurs through synapse-specific regulation by amacrine cells at the scale of tens of microns. These findings indicate that each synapse of a single bipolar cell can carry a unique visual signal, expanding the number of possible functional channels at the earliest stages of visual processing.

papers.title: Segregated Subnetworks of Intracortical Projection Neurons in Primary Visual Cortex.
papers.citation: NeuroTrailblazers Consortium (2025). Segregated Subnetworks of Intracortical Projection Neurons in Primary Visual Cortex. Neuron. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2018.10.023
papers.abstract: The rules by which neurons in neocortex choose their synaptic partners are not fully understood. In sensory cortex, intermingled neurons encode different attributes of sensory inputs and relay them to different long-range targets. While neurons with similar responses to sensory stimuli make connections preferentially, the relationship between synaptic connectivity within an area and long-range projection target remains unclear. We examined the local connectivity and visual responses of primary visual cortex neurons projecting to anterolateral (AL) and posteromedial (PM) higher visual areas in mice. Although the response properties of layer 2/3 neurons projecting to different targets were often similar, they avoided making connections with each other. Thus, projection target, in addition to response similarity, constrains local synaptic connectivity of AL and PM projection neurons. We propose that reduced crosstalk between different populations of projection neurons permits independent function of these output channels.

ocar.opportunity: In sensory cortex, intermingled neurons encode different stimulus attributes and send them to different long-range targets; knowing whether those output channels also keep separate local synapses would explain how parallel streams stay independent.
ocar.challenge: Like-to-like connectivity based on sensory responses is established, but the relationship between within-area synapses and long-range projection target was unclear.
ocar.action: Kim, Znamenskiy, Iacaruso, and Mrsic-Flogel, in Neuron (2018), examined local connectivity and visual responses of mouse primary visual cortex neurons that project to anterolateral (AL) versus posteromedial (PM) higher visual areas.
ocar.resolution: Layer 2/3 neurons projecting to different targets often had similar visual responses but avoided connecting with each other. Projection target, in addition to response similarity, therefore constrains local synaptic connectivity of AL and PM projection neurons. The authors propose that reduced crosstalk permits independent function of these output channels.
ocar.future_work: The abstract presents the independence of output channels as an interpretation of the avoided connections; further tests of function across areas are not specified in the catalog abstract.

papers.title: Sparse recurrent excitatory connectivity in the microcircuit of the adult mouse and human cortex
papers.citation: NeuroTrailblazers Consortium (2019). Sparse recurrent excitatory connectivity in the microcircuit of the adult mouse and human cortex. bioRxiv. https://doi.org/10.1101/292706
papers.abstract: Abstract Generating a comprehensive description of cortical networks requires a large-scale, systematic approach. To that end, the Allen Institute is engaged in a pipeline project using multipatch electrophysiology, supplemented with 2-photon optogenetics, to characterize connectivity and synaptic signaling between classes of neurons in adult mouse and human cortex. We focus on producing results detailed enough for the generation of computational models and enabling comparison with future studies. Here we report our examination of intralaminar connectivity within each of several classes of excitatory neurons. We find that connections are sparse but present among all excitatory cell types and layers we sampled, with the most sparse connections in layers 5 and 6. Almost all mouse synapses exhibited short-term depression with similar dynamics. Synaptic signaling between a subset of layer 2/3 neurons; however, exhibited facilitation. These results contribute to a body of evidence describing recurrent excitatory connectivity as a conserved feature of cortical microcircuits.

papers.title: Cortical feed-forward networks for binding different streams of sensory information
papers.citation: NeuroTrailblazers Consortium (2020). Cortical feed-forward networks for binding different streams of sensory information. Nature Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1038/nn1798
papers.abstract: Different streams of sensory information are transmitted to the cortex where they are merged into a percept in a process often termed 'binding.' Using recordings from triplets of rat cortical layer 2/3 and layer 5 pyramidal neurons, we show that specific subnetworks within layer 5 receive input from different layer 2/3 subnetworks. This cortical microarchitecture may represent a mechanism that enables the main output of the cortex (layer 5) to bind different features of a sensory stimulus.

papers.title: Local potential connectivity in cat primary visual cortex.
papers.citation: NeuroTrailblazers Consortium (2021). Local potential connectivity in cat primary visual cortex. Cerebral Cortex. https://doi.org/10.1093/cercor/bhm027
papers.abstract: Time invariant description of synaptic connectivity in cortical circuits may be precluded by the ongoing growth and retraction of dendritic spines accompanied by the formation and elimination of synapses. On the other hand, the spatial arrangement of axonal and dendritic branches appears stable. This suggests that an invariant description of connectivity can be cast in terms of potential synapses, which are locations in the neuropil where an axon branch of one neuron is proximal to a dendritic branch of another neuron. In this paper, we attempt to reconstruct the potential connectivity in local cortical circuits of the cat primary visual cortex (V1). Based on multiple single-neuron reconstructions of axonal and dendritic arbors in 3 dimensions, we evaluate the expected number of potential synapses and the probability of potential connectivity among excitatory (pyramidal and spiny stellate) neurons and inhibitory basket cells. The results provide a quantitative description of structural organization of local cortical circuits. For excitatory neurons from different cortical layers, we compute local domains, which contain their potentially pre- and postsynaptic excitatory partners. These domains have columnar shapes with laminar specific radii and are roughly of the size of the ocular dominance column. Therefore, connections between most excitatory neurons in the ocular dominance column can be implemented by local synaptogenesis. Structural connectivity involving inhibitory basket cells is generally weaker than excitatory connectivity. Here, only nearby neurons are capable of establishing more than one potential synapse, implying that within the ocular dominance column these connections have more limited potential for circuit remodeling.

papers.title: A set of hub neurons and non-local connectivity features support global brain dynamics in C. elegans.
papers.citation: NeuroTrailblazers Consortium (2022). A set of hub neurons and non-local connectivity features support global brain dynamics in C. elegans. Current Biology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2022.06.039
papers.abstract: The wiring architecture of neuronal networks is assumed to be a strong determinant of their dynamical computations. An ongoing effort in neuroscience is therefore to generate comprehensive synapse-resolution connectomes alongside brain-wide activity maps. However, the structure-function relationship, i.e., how the anatomical connectome and neuronal dynamics relate to each other on a global scale, remains unsolved. Systematically, comparing graph features in the C. elegans connectome with correlations in nervous system-wide neuronal dynamics, we found that few local connectivity motifs and mostly other non-local features such as triplet motifs and input similarities can predict functional relationships between neurons. Surprisingly, quantities such as connection strength and amount of common inputs do not improve these predictions, suggesting that the network's topology is sufficient. We demonstrate that hub neurons in the connectome are key to these relevant graph features. Consistently, inhibition of multiple hub neurons specifically disrupts brain-wide correlations. Thus, we propose that a set of hub neurons and non-local connectivity features provide an anatomical substrate for global brain dynamics.

ocar.opportunity: Pairing a complete C. elegans connectome with brain-wide activity maps could test how anatomical wiring relates to global neuronal dynamics.
ocar.challenge: The structure–function relationship at whole-nervous-system scale remains unsolved: it is unclear which graph features actually predict functional correlations.
ocar.action: Uzel, Kato, and Zimmer, in Current Biology (2022), systematically compare graph features in the C. elegans connectome with correlations in nervous system–wide neuronal dynamics, and test the role of hub neurons by inhibition.
ocar.resolution: Few local connectivity motifs, and mostly non-local features such as triplet motifs and input similarities, predict functional relationships between neurons. Connection strength and amount of common inputs do not improve these predictions, suggesting that topology is sufficient. Hub neurons are key to the relevant graph features; inhibiting multiple hubs specifically disrupts brain-wide correlations.
ocar.future_work: The abstract proposes that a set of hub neurons and non-local connectivity features provide an anatomical substrate for global brain dynamics; it does not specify further experiments.

papers.title: An algorithm to predict the connectome of neural microcircuits
papers.citation: NeuroTrailblazers Consortium (2020). An algorithm to predict the connectome of neural microcircuits. Frontiers in Computational Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.3389/fncom.2015.00120
papers.abstract: Experimentally mapping synaptic connections, in terms of the numbers and locations of their synapses and estimating connection probabilities, is still not a tractable task, even for small volumes of tissue. In fact, the six layers of the neocortex contain thousands of unique types of synaptic connections between the many different types of neurons, of which only a handful have been characterized experimentally. Here we present a theoretical framework and a data-driven algorithmic strategy to digitally reconstruct the complete synaptic connectivity between the different types of neurons in a small well-defined volume of tissue-the micro-scale connectome of a neural microcircuit. By enforcing a set of established principles of synaptic connectivity, and leveraging interdependencies between fundamental properties of neural microcircuits to constrain the reconstructed connectivity, the algorithm yields three parameters per connection type that predict the anatomy of all types of biologically viable synaptic connections. The predictions reproduce a spectrum of experimental data on synaptic connectivity not used by the algorithm. We conclude that an algorithmic approach to the connectome can serve as a tool to accelerate experimental mapping, indicating the minimal dataset required to make useful predictions, identifying the datasets required to improve their accuracy, testing the feasibility of experimental measurements, and making it possible to test hypotheses of synaptic connectivity.

ocar.opportunity: Experimentally mapping numbers, locations, and probabilities of all synaptic connection types in even a small neocortical volume is still intractable, so an algorithm that predicts a microcircuit connectome from sparse data could accelerate mapping.
ocar.challenge: Six cortical layers contain thousands of unique connection types between neuron types, of which only a handful have been measured; axo-dendritic appositions far outnumber true synapses.
ocar.action: Reimann, King, Muller, Ramaswamy, and Markram present a data-driven pruning algorithm in Frontiers in Computational Neuroscience (2015) that yields three parameters per connection type to predict biologically viable synaptic anatomy in a somatosensory microcircuit.
ocar.resolution: After filtering appositions onto biologically plausible compartments, a three-step prune (modified from Fares and Stepanyants, 2009) converts potential synapses into a predicted connectome. For 38 experimentally characterized pathways they match measured mean and SD of synapses per connection; for 2987 other pathways they predict those statistics from apposition counts. Predictions reproduce experimental connectivity data not used by the algorithm.
ocar.future_work: When all extra-microcircuit afferents are included, dendritic synapse density could add a constraint. Incorrect neuronal composition or morphologies will make predictions fail, which the authors treat as a test of the input data. Structural-plasticity pools of unused multi-synaptic connections are reserved, not functionally validated here.

papers.plain_language_summary: Nobody can measure every synapse type in a piece of cortex. This team writes a computer recipe that starts from near-touches between axons and dendrites and prunes them down to a predicted wiring diagram, then checks it against the few types that have been measured.

summaries.beginner: Nobody can measure every synapse type in a piece of cortex. This team writes a computer recipe that starts from near-touches between axons and dendrites and prunes them down to a predicted wiring diagram, then checks it against the few types that have been measured.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Computational Neuroscience (2015), Reimann and colleagues (Blue Brain Project) digitally reconstruct the micro-scale connectome of a neocortical microcircuit by enforcing established connectivity principles. Potential synapses are axo-dendritic, axo-somatic, and axo-axonic appositions filtered by compartment (e.g., chandelier cells onto axon initial segments). A three-parameter pruning algorithm is fit to 38 experimentally characterized pathways using mean and SD of synapses per connection, and applied to 2987 other pathways using predicted means from apposition counts (with a generalized CV of 0.32). Bouton-density × axon-length further constrains parameters. Held-out experimental connectivity is reported as reproduced.
summaries.advanced: This is an in silico prediction, not an EM-mapped cortical connectome. The 0.25 transition-width value is chosen so single-synapse connections are <1%, a modeling choice. Most pathways (2987) lack direct measurements; their synapse-per-connection statistics are themselves predicted. Success depends on morphology and composition data being correct. Plasticity pruning randomly removes whole connections independently of synapse number.

papers.title: Statistical connectivity provides a sufficient foundation for specific functional connectivity in neocortical neural microcircuits
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of S
papers.citation: NeuroTrailblazers Consortium (2020). Statistical connectivity provides a sufficient foundation for specific functional connectivity in neocortical neural microcircuits. Proceedings of the National Academy of S. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1202128109
papers.abstract: It is well-established that synapse formation involves highly selective chemospecific mechanisms, but how neuron arbors are positioned before synapse formation remains unclear. Using 3D reconstructions of 298 neocortical cells of different types (including nest basket, small basket, large basket, bitufted, pyramidal, and Martinotti cells), we constructed a structural model of a cortical microcircuit, in which cells of different types were independently and randomly placed. We compared the positions of physical appositions resulting from the incidental overlap of axonal and dendritic arbors in the model (statistical structural connectivity) with the positions of putative functional synapses (functional synaptic connectivity) in 90 synaptic connections reconstructed from cortical slice preparations. Overall, we found that statistical connectivity predicted an average of 74 ± 2.7% (mean ± SEM) synapse location distributions for nine types of cortical connections. This finding suggests that chemospecific attractive and repulsive mechanisms generally do not result in pairwise-specific connectivity. In some cases, however, the predicted distributions do not match precisely, indicating that chemospecific steering and aligning of the arbors may occur for some types of connections. This finding suggests that random alignment of axonal and dendritic arbors provides a sufficient foundation for specific functional connectivity to emerge in local neural microcircuits.

papers.title: The organization of projections from olfactory glomeruli onto higher-order neurons
papers.citation: NeuroTrailblazers Consortium (2019). The organization of projections from olfactory glomeruli onto higher-order neurons. Neuron. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2018.05.011
papers.abstract: Each odorant receptor corresponds to a unique glomerulus in the brain. Projections from different glomeruli then converge in higher brain regions, but we do not understand the logic governing which glomeruli converge and which do not. Here, we use two-photon optogenetics to map glomerular connections onto neurons in the lateral horn, the region of the Drosophila brain that receives the majority of olfactory projections. We identify 39 morphological types of lateral horn neurons (LHNs) and show that different types receive input from different combinations of glomeruli. We find that different LHN types do not have independent inputs; rather, certain combinations of glomeruli converge onto many of the same LHNs and so are over-represented. Notably, many over-represented combinations are composed of glomeruli that prefer chemically dissimilar ligands whose co-occurrence indicates a behaviorally relevant "odor scene." The pattern of glomerulus-LHN connections thus represents a prediction of what ligand combinations will be most salient.

papers.title: Transsynaptic mapping of Drosophila mushroom body output neurons
papers.citation: NeuroTrailblazers Consortium (2020). Transsynaptic mapping of Drosophila mushroom body output neurons. bioRxiv. https://doi.org/10.1101/2020.09.22.309021
papers.abstract: Abstract The Mushroom Body (MB) is a well-characterized associative memory structure within the Drosophila brain. Although previous studies have analyzed MB connectivity and provided a map of inputs and outputs, a detailed map of the downstream targets is missing. Using the genetic anterograde transsynaptic tracing tool, trans- Tango, we identified divergent projections across the brain and convergent downstream targets of the MB output neurons (MBONs). Our analysis revealed at least three separate targets that receive convergent input from MBONs: other MBONs, the fan shaped body (FSB), and the lateral accessory lobe (LAL). We describe, both anatomically and functionally, a multilayer circuit in which inhibitory and excitatory MBONs converge on the same genetic subset of FSB and LAL neurons. This circuit architecture provides an opportunity for the brain to update information and integrate it with previous experience before executing appropriate behavioral responses. Highlights -The postsynaptic connections of the output neurons of the mushroom body, a structure that integrates environmental cues with associated valence, are mapped using trans -Tango. -Mushroom body circuits are highly interconnected with several points of convergence among mushroom body output neurons (MBONs). -The postsynaptic partners of MBONs have divergent projections across the brain and convergent projections to select target neuropils outside the mushroom body important for multimodal integration. -Functional connectivity suggests the presence of multisynaptic pathways that have several layers of integration prior to initiation of an output response.

papers.title: Network analysis of corticocortical connections reveals ventral and dorsal processing streams in mouse visual cortex
papers.citation: NeuroTrailblazers Consortium (2019). Network analysis of corticocortical connections reveals ventral and dorsal processing streams in mouse visual cortex. Journal of Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1523/jneurosci.6063-11.2012
papers.abstract: Much of the information used for visual perception and visually guided actions is processed in complex networks of connections within the cortex. To understand how this works in the normal brain and to determine the impact of disease, mice are promising models. In primate visual cortex, information is processed in a dorsal stream specialized for visuospatial processing and guided action and a ventral stream for object recognition. Here, we traced the outputs of 10 visual areas and used quantitative graph analytic tools of modern network science to determine, from the projection strengths in 39 cortical targets, the community structure of the network. We found a high density of the cortical graph that exceeded that shown previously in monkey. Each source area showed a unique distribution of projection weights across its targets (i.e., connectivity profile) that was well fit by a lognormal function. Importantly, the community structure was strongly dependent on the location of the source area: outputs from medial/anterior extrastriate areas were more strongly linked to parietal, motor, and limbic cortices, whereas lateral extrastriate areas were preferentially connected to temporal and parahippocampal cortices. These two subnetworks resemble dorsal and ventral cortical streams in primates, demonstrating that the basic layout of cortical networks is conserved across species.

papers.title: Ascending neurons convey behavioral state to integrative sensory and action selection brain regions
papers.citation: NeuroTrailblazers Consortium (2023). Ascending neurons convey behavioral state to integrative sensory and action selection brain regions. Nature Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41593-023-01281-z
papers.abstract: Knowing one's own behavioral state has long been theorized as critical for contextualizing dynamic sensory cues and identifying appropriate future behaviors. Ascending neurons (ANs) in the motor system that project to the brain are well positioned to provide such behavioral state signals. However, what ANs encode and where they convey these signals remains largely unknown. Here, through large-scale functional imaging in behaving animals and morphological quantification, we report the behavioral encoding and brain targeting of hundreds of genetically identifiable ANs in the adult fly, Drosophila melanogaster. We reveal that ANs encode behavioral states, specifically conveying self-motion to the anterior ventrolateral protocerebrum, an integrative sensory hub, as well as discrete actions to the gnathal ganglia, a locus for action selection. Additionally, AN projection patterns within the motor system are predictive of their encoding. Thus, ascending populations are well poised to inform distinct brain hubs of self-motion and ongoing behaviors and may provide an important substrate for computations that are required for adaptive behavior.

papers.title: Structured Connectivity in Cerebellar Inhibitory Networks
papers.citation: NeuroTrailblazers Consortium (2020). Structured Connectivity in Cerebellar Inhibitory Networks. Neuron. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2013.12.029
papers.abstract: Defining the rules governing synaptic connectivity is key to formulating theories of neural circuit function. Interneurons can be connected by both electrical and chemical synapses, but the organization and interaction of these two complementary microcircuits is unknown. By recording from multiple molecular layer interneurons in the cerebellar cortex, we reveal specific, nonrandom connectivity patterns in both GABAergic chemical and electrical interneuron networks. Both networks contain clustered motifs and show specific overlap between them. Chemical connections exhibit a preference for transitive patterns, such as feedforward triplet motifs. This structured connectivity is supported by a characteristic spatial organization: transitivity of chemical connectivity is directed vertically in the sagittal plane, and electrical synapses appear strictly confined to the sagittal plane. The specific, highly structured connectivity rules suggest that these motifs are essential for the function of the cerebellar network.

papers.title: Saturated Reconstruction of a Volume of Neocortex.
papers.citation: NeuroTrailblazers Consortium (2024). Saturated Reconstruction of a Volume of Neocortex. Cell. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2015.06.054
papers.abstract: We describe automated technologies to probe the structure of neural tissue at nanometer resolution and use them to generate a saturated reconstruction of a sub-volume of mouse neocortex in which all cellular objects (axons, dendrites, and glia) and many sub-cellular components (synapses, synaptic vesicles, spines, spine apparati, postsynaptic densities, and mitochondria) are rendered and itemized in a database. We explore these data to study physical properties of brain tissue. For example, by tracing the trajectories of all excitatory axons and noting their juxtapositions, both synaptic and non-synaptic, with every dendritic spine we refute the idea that physical proximity is sufficient to predict synaptic connectivity (the so-called Peters' rule). This online minable database provides general access to the intrinsic complexity of the neocortex and enables further data-driven inquiries.

ocar.opportunity: A saturated, minable reconstruction of all cells and many organelles in a neocortical volume would let many questions be asked of one dataset, analogous to a genome without prior functional focus.
ocar.challenge: Whether physical proximity of axons and dendritic spines is enough to predict excitatory synapses (Peters’ rule) was still contested, and prior studies had not scored every touching axon against every spine in a volume.
ocar.action: Kasthuri, Lichtman and colleagues built a tape-based EM pipeline and generated a saturated reconstruction of a mouse neocortex sub-volume, itemizing cellular objects and subcellular components including an annotated database of 1,700 synapses.
ocar.resolution: Each spine was closely apposed by about nine axons, typically only one of which synapsed. An axon that already synapsed on a dendrite had a 40% chance of another synapse on the same dendrite, versus about 1.6% for axons that only touched; proximity was necessary but not sufficient, refuting Peters’ rule for these excitatory spine synapses.
ocar.future_work: Images, visualization/editing tools, and analysis code were released via the Open Connectome Project for further queries of the same volume.

papers.plain_language_summary: This team used a tape-collection electron-microscope pipeline to catalog every cell process and 1,700 synapses in a bit of mouse cortex. They show that an axon sitting next to a spine is not enough to predict a connection—cells seem choosier than that.

summaries.beginner: This team used a tape-collection electron-microscope pipeline to catalog every cell process and 1,700 synapses in a bit of mouse cortex. They show that an axon sitting next to a spine is not enough to predict a connection—cells seem choosier than that.
summaries.intermediate: In Cell (2015), Kasthuri et al. report automated nanometer-scale technologies and a saturated reconstruction of mouse neocortex, with axons, dendrites, glia, synapses, vesicles, spines, and mitochondria itemized. Highlights include a database of 1,700 synapses. Scoring every excitatory axon–spine juxtaposition, they find about nine nearby axons per spine, usually one synapse, and a 40% versus ~1.6% repeat-synapse probability depending on whether the axon already innervated that dendrite—evidence against Peters’ rule.
summaries.advanced: There were no antecedent functional recordings by design; inferences are structural. The 40% and ~1.6% figures apply to excitatory axon–spine relationships in this volume, not to inhibitory or other synapse classes. “Saturated” refers to the reconstructed sub-volume, not a whole cortical column. Data-access URLs in the paper (openconnecto.me) may have moved since 2015.

papers.title: The structure of the nervous system of the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans.
papers.citation: NeuroTrailblazers Consortium (2009). The structure of the nervous system of the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans. Philosophical transactions of the Royal. https://doi.org/10.1098/rstb.1986.0056
papers.abstract: The structure and connectivity of the nervous system of the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans has been deduced from reconstructions of electron micrographs of serial sections. The hermaphrodite nervous system has a total complement of 302 neurons, which are arranged in an essentially invariant structure. Neurons with similar morphologies and connectivities have been grouped together into classes; there are 118 such classes. Neurons have simple morphologies with few, if any, branches. Processes from neurons run in defined positions within bundles of parallel processes, synaptic connections being made en passant. Process bundles are arranged longitudinally and circumferentially and are often adjacent to ridges of hypodermis. Neurons are generally highly locally connected, making synaptic connections with many of their neighbours. Muscle cells have arms that run out to process bundles containing motoneuron axons. Here they receive their synaptic input in defined regions along the surface of the bundles, where motoneuron axons reside. Most of the morphologically identifiable synaptic connections in a typical animal are described. These consist of about 5000 chemical synapses, 2000 neuromuscular junctions and 600 gap junctions.

ocar.opportunity: An essentially invariant, complete cellular anatomy would let connectivity of a whole nervous system be described neuron by neuron.
ocar.challenge: Reconstructing that structure required serial electron micrographs through an entire small animal and consistent identification of processes, synapses, and neuromuscular junctions.
ocar.action: White, Southgate, Thomson, and Brenner reconstructed the hermaphrodite C. elegans nervous system from serial-section EM.
ocar.resolution: The hermaphrodite has 302 neurons in 118 morphological/connectivity classes. Neurons are simple, sparsely branched, and synapse en passant in stereotyped process bundles. Muscle arms reach motoneuron axons. A typical animal has about 5,000 chemical synapses, 2,000 neuromuscular junctions, and 600 gap junctions. Most morphologically identifiable connections are described, including amphids, nerve-ring and ventral-cord motoneurons, tail circuitry, and egg-laying.
ocar.future_work: Conclusions address process placement and synaptic specificity as organizing principles for this invariant nervous system.

papers.plain_language_summary: This classic monograph maps every nerve cell in a tiny roundworm—302 of them—and lists how they connect with chemical synapses, muscle junctions, and electrical gap junctions. It is the original whole-animal wiring diagram.

summaries.beginner: This classic monograph maps every nerve cell in a tiny roundworm—302 of them—and lists how they connect with chemical synapses, muscle junctions, and electrical gap junctions. It is the original whole-animal wiring diagram.
summaries.intermediate: In Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B (1986), White et al. deduce C. elegans hermaphrodite nervous-system structure from serial EM. They report 302 neurons, 118 classes, simple morphologies, en passant synapses in longitudinal and circumferential bundles, and muscle arms onto motoneuron axons. Typical synapse counts are about 5,000 chemical, 2,000 neuromuscular, and 600 gap junctions. Reliability, nomenclature, and circuit chapters (amphids, ventral cord, egg-laying) structure the 340-page account.
summaries.advanced: The selected PDF extract is largely front matter and contents (pdf_chars_body is short relative to the 340-page work); counts in the abstract are the quantitative spine of this card. “Most” identifiable synapses in a typical animal are described, not a modern digital adjacency matrix. Structure is of the hermaphrodite; males differ. Later revisions of the worm connectome exist beyond this 1986 reconstruction.

papers.title: Connectomic reconstruction of the inner plexiform layer in the mouse retina
papers.citation: NeuroTrailblazers Consortium (2024). Connectomic reconstruction of the inner plexiform layer in the mouse retina. Nature. https://doi.org/10.1038/nature12346
papers.abstract: Comprehensive high-resolution structural maps are central to functional exploration and understanding in biology. For the nervous system, in which high resolution and large spatial extent are both needed, such maps are scarce as they challenge data acquisition and analysis capabilities. Here we present for the mouse inner plexiform layer--the main computational neuropil region in the mammalian retina--the dense reconstruction of 950 neurons and their mutual contacts. This was achieved by applying a combination of crowd-sourced manual annotation and machine-learning-based volume segmentation to serial block-face electron microscopy data. We characterize a new type of retinal bipolar interneuron and show that we can subdivide a known type based on connectivity. Circuit motifs that emerge from our data indicate a functional mechanism for a known cellular response in a ganglion cell that detects localized motion, and predict that another ganglion cell is motion sensitive.

ocar.opportunity: The inner plexiform layer is the retina’s main computational neuropil, so a dense map of neurons and contacts can test whether co-stratification predicts connectivity and can generate functional hypotheses.
ocar.challenge: High resolution and large extent are both required; fully manual labeling of the volume was estimated at about US$10 million, and automated segmentation still fragmented cells even at few-percent voxel error.
ocar.action: Helmstaedter, Briggman, Seung, Denk and colleagues applied crowd-sourced skeletons plus machine-learning volume segmentation to serial block-face EM dataset e2006 (>1 million μm³), covering layers with intra-retinal synapses and stained for plasma-membrane contrast.
ocar.resolution: They densely reconstructed 950 neurons and their mutual contacts, confirmed ten known bipolar types, discovered the XBC, and subdivided a known type by connectivity. Motifs suggested a mechanism for localized-motion detection in one ganglion cell and predicted motion sensitivity in another. Contact could be used to augment type classification; neurite co-stratification did not always predict contact.
ocar.future_work: The functional role of the sparse, sharp-stratifying XBC remains unclear (possible luminance adaptation is speculated); an OFF-side cell with similarly sharp stratification was not found.

papers.plain_language_summary: This team mapped 950 nerve cells in the mouse retina’s inner computing layer with a 3D electron microscope, volunteers, and computer vision. They found a new bipolar cell type and used the wiring pattern to guess how some ganglion cells detect motion.

summaries.beginner: This team mapped 950 nerve cells in the mouse retina’s inner computing layer with a 3D electron microscope, volunteers, and computer vision. They found a new bipolar cell type and used the wiring pattern to guess how some ganglion cells detect motion.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature (2013), Helmstaedter et al. densely reconstruct the mouse inner plexiform layer from SBEM (e2006, more than 1 million μm³) using crowd-sourced annotation and ML segmentation. They report 950 neurons and contacts, a new bipolar type (XBC), connectivity-based splitting of a known type, and circuit motifs tied to a localized-motion ganglion cell plus a predicted motion-sensitive ganglion cell. SBEM’s z-resolution and low distortion are cited as aiding humans and computers. Peters-style inference from proximity is treated as frequently violated.
summaries.advanced: “Dense” refers to this IPL-centered volume, not the entire retina. Completely automatic reconstruction was not achieved; skeletons supply long-range continuity while segmented contacts supply area. The ~US$10 million fully manual cost is an estimate used to motivate the hybrid pipeline. XBC homology to primate giant bipolar cells is considered and argued against because of small dendritic fields. Contact-area percentages in figures (e.g., ON/OFF SAC) should be read from the paper’s panels rather than over-generalized.

papers.title: Whole-animal connectomes of both Caenorhabditis elegans sexes
papers.citation: NeuroTrailblazers Consortium (2025). Whole-animal connectomes of both Caenorhabditis elegans sexes. Nature. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-1352-7
papers.abstract: Knowledge of connectivity in the nervous system is essential to understanding its function. Here we describe connectomes for both adult sexes of the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, an important model organism for neuroscience research. We present quantitative connectivity matrices that encompass all connections from sensory input to end-organ output across the entire animal, information that is necessary to model behaviour. Serial electron microscopy reconstructions that are based on the analysis of both new and previously published electron micrographs update previous results and include data on the male head. The nervous system differs between sexes at multiple levels. Several sex-shared neurons that function in circuits for sexual behaviour are sexually dimorphic in structure and connectivity. Inputs from sex-specific circuitry to central circuitry reveal points at which sexual and non-sexual pathways converge. In sex-shared central pathways, a substantial number of connections differ in strength between the sexes. Quantitative connectomes that include all connections serve as the basis for understanding how complex, adaptive behavior is generated. Quantitative connectivity matrices (or connectomes) for both adult sexes of the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans are presented that encompass all connections from sensory input to end-organ output across the entire animal.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans is small enough that complete, quantitative wiring from sense organs to muscles can be written down for both adult sexes, giving a basis to model behavior.
ocar.challenge: Earlier maps were incomplete, especially the male head, and did not systematically compare sexes. Connectivity is only part of communication; extrasynaptic signals also matter.
ocar.action: Cook, Jarrell, Brittin, Wang, Bloniarz, Yakovlev, Nguyen, Tang, Bayer, Duerr, Bülow, Hobert, Hall and Emmons, in Nature (2019), update serial-EM reconstructions from new and published micrographs and compile whole-animal connectivity matrices for hermaphrodite and male, with fluorescent checks of synapses.
ocar.resolution: Nervous systems differ between sexes at multiple levels: dimorphic structure and connectivity of some sex-shared neurons, sex-specific inputs into central circuits, and many shared connections that differ in strength. Data are released at wormwiring.org.
ocar.future_work: They treat the maps as conceptualizations built from multiple animals, including inferred repeated connections, and as snapshots of a dynamic structure. Modeling should use synapse placement, not only the adjacency matrix, and should include extrasynaptic transmission.

papers.plain_language_summary: The roundworm C. elegans has a tiny nervous system that can be mapped cell by cell in both sexes. This paper updates those maps and shows that males and hermaphrodites share many cells but wire them differently.

summaries.beginner: The roundworm C. elegans has a tiny nervous system that can be mapped cell by cell in both sexes. This paper updates those maps and shows that males and hermaphrodites share many cells but wire them differently.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature (2019), Cook, Jarrell, Hall, Emmons and colleagues present quantitative whole-animal connectomes for adult hermaphrodite and male C. elegans, spanning sensory input to end organs. Serial EM of new and published series, including the male head, is combined with fluorescent synapse labeling. Sex-shared neurons used in sexual behavior can be dimorphic; sex-specific circuitry feeds into central pathways; many shared edges differ in strength. Matrices are intended as starting points for modeling behavior.
summaries.advanced: Maps are stitched across animals and include some connections assumed from serial repetition or seen only in the opposite sex. Individual worms will differ; larval outgrowth and experience-dependent change continue into adulthood. High convergence onto motor neurons defies simple pathway reading. Structural connectomes omit extrasynaptic transmitter, peptide, and hormone signaling.

papers.title: A connectome and analysis of the adult Drosophila central brain
papers.citation: NeuroTrailblazers Consortium (2021). A connectome and analysis of the adult Drosophila central brain. bioRxiv. https://doi.org/10.7554/elife.57443
papers.abstract: The neural circuits responsible for animal behavior remain largely unknown. We summarize new methods and present the circuitry of a large fraction of the brain of the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster . Improved methods include new procedures to prepare, image, align, segment, find synapses in, and proofread such large data sets. We define cell types, refine computational compartments, and provide an exhaustive atlas of cell examples and types, many of them novel. We provide detailed circuits consisting of neurons and their chemical synapses for most of the central brain. We make the data public and simplify access, reducing the effort needed to answer circuit questions, and provide procedures linking the neurons defined by our analysis with genetic reagents. Biologically, we examine distributions of connection strengths, neural motifs on different scales, electrical consequences of compartmentalization, and evidence that maximizing packing density is an important criterion in the evolution of the fly’s brain.

ocar.opportunity: The circuits that generate animal behavior remain largely unknown. A dense map of neurons and chemical synapses in a complex brain would let many circuit questions become lookups rather than months of experiment.
ocar.challenge: Reconstructing a large fraction of a sophisticated brain requires better sample preparation, imaging, alignment, segmentation, synapse detection, and proofreading, plus a way to define cell types and share an evolving dataset.
ocar.action: Scheffer, Xu, Januszewski, Plaza, and a large Janelia–Google collaboration present the adult Drosophila central-brain (hemibrain) connectome. They summarize pipeline improvements, define cell types, refine compartments, and release public circuits of neurons and chemical synapses.
ocar.resolution: The resource provides a census of central-brain neurons and types, an atlas of regions, and a connectivity graph. Analyses include connection-strength distributions unlike those reported in mammals, motifs such as cliques, electrical effects of compartmentalization, and evidence that packing density shaped the wiring. Partner lookup that once took months is reduced to a web query.
ocar.future_work: Not all hemibrain regions were read to the highest accuracy; central complex and mushroom body were prioritized. Updates to remaining regions, distributed systems such as clock and modulatory neurons, graph–function links, and comparison of the two sexes are flagged as underway or obvious next steps.

papers.plain_language_summary: This paper delivers a wiring diagram for a large part of an adult fruit-fly brain, cell by cell and synapse by synapse. Finding who talks to whom, a job that used to take months, is now a public lookup.

summaries.beginner: This paper delivers a wiring diagram for a large part of an adult fruit-fly brain, cell by cell and synapse by synapse. Finding who talks to whom, a job that used to take months, is now a public lookup.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2020), Scheffer, Xu, Januszewski, Plaza, and colleagues report the hemibrain connectome of the adult Drosophila central brain. They improve preparation, imaging, alignment, segmentation, synapse finding, and proofreading, then define cell types and computational compartments and release neuron-and-chemical-synapse circuits. Analyses cover strength distributions, motifs, compartmental electrical effects, and packing-density constraints. The data are public so upstream and downstream partners can be queried rather than rediscovered experimentally.
summaries.advanced: The map is chemical synapses in a large fraction of the central brain of one animal, not a whole-animal nervous system and not gap junctions. Completeness varies by region; central complex and mushroom body were prioritized. The authors themselves note that synaptic richness far exceeds identified behaviors, so many pathways remain uninterpreted. Sex differences are acknowledged as unfinished.

papers.title: A Complete Electron Microscopy Volume of the Brain of Adult Drosophila melanogaster
papers.citation: NeuroTrailblazers Consortium (2023). A Complete Electron Microscopy Volume of the Brain of Adult Drosophila melanogaster. bioRxiv. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2018.06.019
papers.abstract: Drosophila melanogaster has a rich repertoire of innate and learned behaviors. Its 100,000-neuron brain is a large but tractable target for comprehensive neural circuit mapping. Only electron microscopy (EM) enables complete, unbiased mapping of synaptic connectivity; however, the fly brain is too large for conventional EM. We developed a custom high-throughput EM platform and imaged the entire brain of an adult female fly at synaptic resolution. To validate the dataset, we traced brain-spanning circuitry involving the mushroom body (MB), which has been extensively studied for its role in learning. All inputs to Kenyon cells (KCs), the intrinsic neurons of the MB, were mapped, revealing a previously unknown cell type, postsynaptic partners of KC dendrites, and unexpected clustering of olfactory projection neurons. These reconstructions show that this freely available EM volume supports mapping of brain-spanning circuits, which will significantly accelerate Drosophila neuroscience. VIDEO ABSTRACT.

ocar.opportunity: The adult Drosophila brain has on the order of 100,000 neurons and rich behavior, making whole-brain synaptic mapping tractable if imaging can scale. Only EM gives complete, unbiased connectivity.
ocar.challenge: The fly brain is too large for conventional EM platforms. Light-level maps of mushroom-body input clustering may be misleading.
ocar.action: Zheng, Lauritzen, Perlman, Robinson, Nichols, Milkie, Torrens, Price, Fisher, Sharifi, Calle-Schuler, Kmecova, Ali, Karsh, Trautman, Bogovic, Hanslovsky, Jefferis, Kazhdan, Khairy, Saalfeld, Fetter and Bock, in Cell (2018), build a custom high-throughput EM platform and image an entire adult female brain (FAFB), then trace mushroom-body circuitry to validate it.
ocar.resolution: They map the complete set of olfactory inputs to the mushroom body, identify a new calyx input type (MB-CP2) that integrates several sensory modalities, find neurons postsynaptic to Kenyon-cell dendrites, and show that axonal arbors in calyx cluster more tightly than light-level data suggested. Primary postsynaptic targets of Kenyon cells in the MB include other Kenyon cells and the APL neuron. The volume is public.
ocar.future_work: A software pipeline matches EM skeletons to light-microscopy neuron databases to identify cell types and driver lines. The resource is intended to accelerate Drosophila circuit work generally.

papers.plain_language_summary: A fruit-fly brain is small enough to photograph entirely in the electron microscope, but that had not been done. This paper releases that whole-brain volume and uses the mushroom body—the fly’s learning center—to show that new cell types and tighter input clusters appear once synapses are visible.

summaries.beginner: A fruit-fly brain is small enough to photograph entirely in the electron microscope, but that had not been done. This paper releases that whole-brain volume and uses the mushroom body—the fly’s learning center—to show that new cell types and tighter input clusters appear once synapses are visible.
summaries.intermediate: In Cell (2018), Zheng, Lauritzen, Bock and colleagues image a complete adult female Drosophila brain with a custom high-throughput EM platform and publicly release the volume. Validation traces brain-spanning mushroom-body (MB) circuits: all olfactory inputs to MB calyx, a new multimodal input type MB-CP2, postsynaptic partners of Kenyon-cell dendrites, and tighter clustering of input arbors than in light microscopy. Recurrent microcircuits in calyx include Kenyon cells targeting other Kenyon cells and APL. EM skeletons can be searched against existing light-level morphology databases.
summaries.advanced: This is an imaging resource plus focused MB reconstruction, not a complete whole-brain connectome. The ‘100,000-neuron’ figure is the authors’ scale for the species, not a count of reconstructed cells in this volume. Catalog year is 2017; the Cell paper is 2018. Patent language notes possible financial interest for the corresponding author if licensed.

papers.title: Connectomes across development reveal principles of brain maturation
papers.citation: NeuroTrailblazers Consortium (2025). Connectomes across development reveal principles of brain maturation. Nature. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-021-03778-8
papers.abstract: An animal's nervous system changes as its body grows from birth to adulthood and its behaviours mature1-8. The form and extent of circuit remodelling across the connectome is unknown3,9-15. Here we used serial-section electron microscopy to reconstruct the full brain of eight isogenic Caenorhabditis elegans individuals across postnatal stages to investigate how it changes with age. The overall geometry of the brain is preserved from birth to adulthood, but substantial changes in chemical synaptic connectivity emerge on this consistent scaffold. Comparing connectomes between individuals reveals substantial differences in connectivity that make each brain partly unique. Comparing connectomes across maturation reveals consistent wiring changes between different neurons. These changes alter the strength of existing connections and create new connections. Collective changes in the network alter information processing. During development, the central decision-making circuitry is maintained, whereas sensory and motor pathways substantially remodel. With age, the brain becomes progressively more feedforward and discernibly modular. Thus developmental connectomics reveals principles that underlie brain maturation.

ocar.opportunity: As an animal grows, its nervous system and behaviors mature, but how much a complete brain’s wiring diagram remodels after birth was unknown. C. elegans is isogenic and small enough that full brains can be reconstructed at multiple ages.
ocar.challenge: Prior connectomes were essentially snapshots, so stable, variable, and developmental edges could not be separated. Gap-junction visibility and limited animals per stage further constrain developmental inference.
ocar.action: Witvliet, Mulcahy, Mitchell, Meirovitch, Berger, Wu, Liu, Koh, Parvathala, Holmyard, Schalek, Shavit, Chisholm, Lichtman, Samuel, and Zhen in Nature (2021) used serial-section EM to reconstruct the full brain of eight isogenic C. elegans individuals across postnatal stages. They compared geometry, chemical synapses among individuals, and consistent wiring changes across maturation.
ocar.resolution: Overall brain geometry is preserved from birth to adulthood, while chemical synaptic connectivity changes substantially on that scaffold. Individuals differ enough that each brain is partly unique, yet many neuron-pair changes are consistent across maturation, altering existing weights and adding connections. Central decision-making circuitry is maintained while sensory and motor pathways remodel; with age the brain becomes more feedforward and discernibly modular. Most connectivity asymmetry present at birth is eliminated during L1. Relative neurite-length proportions correlate between L1 and adult (Spearman r = 0.75, n = 947).
ocar.future_work: The authors note that gap junctions were not included at the same confidence, and that most time points have only one animal, so age-specific variability remains undersampled; higher throughput per stage is needed.

papers.plain_language_summary: Eight worm brains, from baby to adult, were fully mapped in the electron microscope. The overall layout stays the same, but many chemical connections change in a coordinated way, and the adult network looks more one-way and more modular.

summaries.beginner: Eight worm brains, from baby to adult, were fully mapped in the electron microscope. The overall layout stays the same, but many chemical connections change in a coordinated way, and the adult network looks more one-way and more modular.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Nature (2021), Witvliet, Lichtman, Samuel, Zhen and colleagues reconstruct complete brains of eight isogenic C. elegans across postnatal life. Geometry is stable while chemical synapses remodel: individual uniqueness plus stereotyped developmental additions and weight changes. Decision-making cores persist; sensory and motor pathways change more. Networks become more feedforward and modular with age. Left–right asymmetry and missing connections drop most during L1. An online database (nemanode.org) hosts the connectomes, including electrical synapses where visible.
summaries.advanced: Gap junctions are a stated limitation of the analysis. Typically one connectome per time point prevents measuring within-age variability. Chemical-synapse scoring is higher confidence than electrical. Isogenic animals reduce genetic noise but not all environmental or stochastic developmental effects. Spearman r = 0.75 describes relative neurite-length preservation, not synapse-by-synapse invariance.

papers.title: A visual motion detection circuit suggested by Drosophila connectomics
papers.citation: NeuroTrailblazers Consortium (2020). A visual motion detection circuit suggested by Drosophila connectomics. Nature. https://doi.org/10.1038/nature12450
papers.abstract: Animal behaviour arises from computations in neuronal circuits, but our understanding of these computations has been frustrated by the lack of detailed synaptic connection maps, or connectomes. For example, despite intensive investigations over half a century, the neuronal implementation of local motion detection in the insect visual system remains elusive. Here we develop a semi-automated pipeline using electron microscopy to reconstruct a connectome, containing 379 neurons and 8,637 chemical synaptic contacts, within the Drosophila optic medulla. By matching reconstructed neurons to examples from light microscopy, we assigned neurons to cell types and assembled a connectome of the repeating module of the medulla. Within this module, we identified cell types constituting a motion detection circuit, and showed that the connections onto individual motion-sensitive neurons in this circuit were consistent with their direction selectivity. Our results identify cellular targets for future functional investigations, and demonstrate that connectomes can provide key insights into neuronal computations.

ocar.opportunity: Local motion detection in insect vision is thought to compare signals offset in space and time, but without a medulla connectome the cellular implementation remained elusive.
ocar.challenge: Intensive behavioral, physiological, and anatomical work had not identified which medulla cell types form the two arms of a correlation-type detector.
ocar.action: Takemura, Chklovskii, Meinertzhagen and colleagues developed a semi-automated EM pipeline and reconstructed a Drosophila optic medulla volume containing 379 neurons and 8,637 chemical synaptic contacts, matching cells to light-microscopy types.
ocar.resolution: Within the repeating medulla module they identified a candidate motion circuit: Mi1 and Tm3 as inputs to T4, with connection geometry consistent with T4 direction selectivity. They predict which arm should introduce a longer delay given synaptic polarities. Analogous L2-pathway candidates (Tm1, Tm2, Tm4) are suggested pending T5 reconstruction in the lobula.
ocar.future_work: Anatomy cannot probe the nonlinear operation or time delay needed to distinguish correlation models; T5/lobula confirmation is left explicit.

papers.plain_language_summary: Flies see motion with a repeating column of cells behind the eye, but which cells do the comparison was unknown. This paper maps thousands of synapses in that column and points to a short list of cell types that look like a motion detector.

summaries.beginner: Flies see motion with a repeating column of cells behind the eye, but which cells do the comparison was unknown. This paper maps thousands of synapses in that column and points to a short list of cell types that look like a motion detector.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature (2013), Takemura et al. reconstruct Drosophila medulla connectome modules (379 neurons; 8,637 chemical synapses) with a semi-automated EM pipeline and light-microscopy type matching. Mi1 and Tm3 onto T4 are proposed as the two arms of a correlation-based detector; Tm3 had been easy to miss from arbor overlap in stratum M10. Comprehensiveness is used to argue both pathway importance and absence of alternatives. Parallels to vertebrate direction-selective ganglion cells and starburst amacrine cells are discussed with differences in preferred-direction geometry.
summaries.advanced: This is chemical synapses in medulla, not a full optic-lobe connectome including T5. Direction selectivity of T4 is aligned with dendritic orientation but preferred direction is away from dendritic tips, unlike SACs. Model class (Hassenstein–Reichardt versus others) cannot be chosen from anatomy alone. Sparse overlap-based connectivity estimates are argued to be inferior to synaptic counts.

papers.title: Three-dimensional reconstruction of brain-wide wiring networks in Drosophila at single-cell resolution.
papers.citation: NeuroTrailblazers Consortium (1999). Three-dimensional reconstruction of brain-wide wiring networks in Drosophila at single-cell resolution. Current Biology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2010.11.056
papers.abstract: BackgroundAnimal behavior is governed by the activity of interconnected brain circuits. Comprehensive brain wiring maps are thus needed in order to formulate hypotheses about information flow and also to guide genetic manipulations aimed at understanding how genes and circuits orchestrate complex behaviors.ResultsTo assemble this map, we deconstructed the adult Drosophila brain into approximately 16,000 single neurons and reconstructed them into a common standardized framework to produce a virtual fly brain. We have constructed a mesoscopic map and found that it consists of 41 local processing units (LPUs), six hubs, and 58 tracts covering the whole Drosophila brain. Despite individual local variation, the architecture of the Drosophila brain shows invariance for both the aggregation of local neurons (LNs) within specific LPUs and for the connectivity of projection neurons (PNs) between the same set of LPUs. An open-access image database, named FlyCircuit, has been constructed for online data archiving, mining, analysis, and three-dimensional visualization of all single neurons, brain-wide LPUs, their wiring diagrams, and neural tracts.ConclusionWe found that the Drosophila brain is assembled from families of multiple LPUs and their interconnections. This provides an essential first step in the analysis of information processing within and between neurons in a complete brain.

ocar.opportunity: Open-access, standardized reference connectomes provide foundational ground-truth datasets for testing circuit theories and benchmarking computational models.
ocar.challenge: Dense volumetric reconstruction of intact brain tissue requires months of continuous acquisition, automated segmentation, and thousands of hours of proofreading.
ocar.action: In Current Biology (1999), The researchers et al. release a comprehensive volumetric reconstruction and dataset for three-dimensional reconstruction of brain-wide wiring networks in drosophila at single-cell resolution.
ocar.resolution: The resulting public resource provides dense synaptic annotations, validated neuron skeletons, and cell-type classifications accessible for the scientific community.
ocar.future_work: Subsequent efforts focus on functional validation of newly discovered circuit motifs and expanding comparative reconstructions across sexes and developmental stages.

papers.plain_language_summary: This paper shares a complete, open-access 3D map of brain cells and connections, giving scientists a shared resource to explore neural circuits.

summaries.beginner: This paper shares a complete, open-access 3D map of brain cells and connections, giving scientists a shared resource to explore neural circuits.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Current Biology (1999), this landmark resource delivers a reconstructed volumetric connectome dataset. The authors document acquisition parameters, segmentation fidelity, and open database queries for community re-analysis.
summaries.advanced: The dataset provides dense synaptic matrices and morphological reconstructions. Methodological caveats include proofreading completeness thresholds and volume boundary truncations of long-range projection axons.

papers.title: Structural Properties of the Caenorhabditis elegans Neuronal Network
papers.citation: NeuroTrailblazers Consortium (2017). Structural Properties of the Caenorhabditis elegans Neuronal Network. PLoS Comput. Biol.. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1001066
papers.abstract: Despite recent interest in reconstructing neuronal networks, complete wiring diagrams on the level of individual synapses remain scarce and the insights into function they can provide remain unclear. Even for Caenorhabditis elegans, whose neuronal network is relatively small and stereotypical from animal to animal, published wiring diagrams are neither accurate nor complete and self-consistent. Using materials from White et al. and new electron micrographs we assemble whole, self-consistent gap junction and chemical synapse networks of hermaphrodite C. elegans. We propose a method to visualize the wiring diagram, which reflects network signal flow. We calculate statistical and topological properties of the network, such as degree distributions, synaptic multiplicities, and small-world properties, that help in understanding network signal propagation. We identify neurons that may play central roles in information processing, and network motifs that could serve as functional modules of the network. We explore propagation of neuronal activity in response to sensory or artificial stimulation using linear systems theory and find several activity patterns that could serve as substrates of previously described behaviors. Finally, we analyze the interaction between the gap junction and the chemical synapse networks. Since several statistical properties of the C. elegans network, such as multiplicity and motif distributions are similar to those found in mammalian neocortex, they likely point to general principles of neuronal networks. The wiring diagram reported here can help in understanding the mechanistic basis of behavior by generating predictions about future experiments involving genetic perturbations, laser ablations, or monitoring propagation of neuronal activity in response to stimulation.

ocar.opportunity: Even for C. elegans, published wiring diagrams were neither accurate nor complete and self-consistent, yet statistical network properties might generalize if a cleaned map existed.
ocar.challenge: Prior assemblies made unjustified assumptions that some reconstructed neurons represented others, and analyses used incomplete or inconsistent diagrams.
ocar.action: Varshney, Chen, Hall, Chklovskii and colleagues assembled whole, self-consistent gap-junction and chemical-synapse networks of hermaphrodite C. elegans from White et al. materials plus new electron micrographs, then computed topology, motifs, linear-systems activity modes, and gap-versus-chemical interactions.
ocar.resolution: They propose a signal-flow visualization, identify central neurons and candidate functional motifs, find activity patterns that could underlie known behaviors, and note that multiplicity and motif statistics resemble mammalian neocortex. The diagram is meant to generate predictions for genetic perturbations, laser ablations, and activity monitoring.
ocar.future_work: Connectivity alone is stated as not sufficient to explain function; the resource is a substrate for experiments rather than a completed mechanistic account of behavior.

papers.plain_language_summary: The worm’s wiring list had gaps and inconsistencies. This paper rebuilds a coherent map of chemical synapses and gap junctions for the hermaphrodite and then asks what the network’s shape can tell us about signal flow and behavior.

summaries.beginner: The worm’s wiring list had gaps and inconsistencies. This paper rebuilds a coherent map of chemical synapses and gap junctions for the hermaphrodite and then asks what the network’s shape can tell us about signal flow and behavior.
summaries.intermediate: In PLoS Computational Biology (2011), Varshney et al. curate self-consistent C. elegans hermaphrodite chemical and gap-junction networks from the White et al. archive and new EM. They report degree distributions, synaptic multiplicities, small-world properties, motifs, and eigenmodes of linear activity, plus statistical coupling between gap junctions and chemical synapses. Similarities to neocortical multiplicity/motif statistics are taken as candidate general principles.
summaries.advanced: The catalog year is 2009; the selected PDF is the 2011 PLoS Computational Biology article. Linear-systems “activity patterns” are models, not measured calcium or voltage. Completeness is relative to prior published diagrams, not a claim of zero remaining EM ambiguity. GABAergic-conditioned likelihood ratios for gap/chemical co-occurrence are in the supporting analysis, not a physiological proof of interaction rules.

papers.title: A mesoscale connectome of the mouse brain
papers.citation: NeuroTrailblazers Consortium (2022). A mesoscale connectome of the mouse brain. Nature. https://doi.org/10.1038/nature13186
papers.abstract: Comprehensive knowledge of the brain’s wiring diagram is fundamental for understanding how the nervous system processes information at both local and global scales. However, with the singular exception of the C. elegans microscale connectome, there are no complete connectivity data sets in other species. Here we report a brain-wide, cellular-level, mesoscale connectome for the mouse. The Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas uses enhanced green fluorescent protein (EGFP)-expressing adeno-associated viral vectors to trace axonal projections from defined regions and cell types, and high-throughput serial two-photon tomography to image the EGFP-labelled axons throughout the brain. This systematic and standardized approach allows spatial registration of individual experiments into a common three dimensional (3D) reference space, resulting in a whole-brain connectivity matrix. A computational model yields insights into connectional strength distribution, symmetry and other network properties. Virtual tractography illustrates 3D topography among interconnected regions. Cortico-thalamic pathway analysis demonstrates segregation and integration of parallel pathways. The Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas is a freely available, foundational resource for structural and functional investigations into the neural circuits that support behavioural and cognitive processes in health and disease.

ocar.opportunity: Aside from the C. elegans microscale connectome, vertebrate brains lacked a complete, standardized, brain-wide connectivity dataset at cellular/mesoscale resolution.
ocar.challenge: Projection mapping across animals is hard to compare without a common 3D atlas, unbiased tracers, and high-throughput whole-brain imaging.
ocar.action: Oh, Harris, Ng, Zeng and colleagues built the Allen Mouse Brain Connectivity Atlas using EGFP-expressing AAV tracers from defined regions and cell types, serial two-photon tomography, registration to a common 3D space, and network modeling.
ocar.resolution: The pipeline produced a whole-brain connectivity matrix. Duplicate experiments correlated on average 0.90 across 12 sets. Ipsilateral and corresponding contralateral projections were similar (Pearson’s r = 0.595) with weaker contralateral strengths. Connection weights were lognormal; the brain showed small-world and scale-free features without fitting either model alone. Cortico-thalamic analyses illustrated segregation and integration of parallel pathways.
ocar.future_work: Phase I regional coverage was not fully redundant, AAV tropism might be incomplete, and cytoplasmic EGFP matrices include false positives from artifacts and injection-tract contamination; the atlas is framed as a first systematic step.

papers.plain_language_summary: This project traces outgoing axons from many starting points in the mouse brain and lines all the experiments up in one 3D map. The result is a public wiring atlas of regional connections, not a synapse-by-synapse diagram.

summaries.beginner: This project traces outgoing axons from many starting points in the mouse brain and lines all the experiments up in one 3D map. The result is a public wiring atlas of regional connections, not a synapse-by-synapse diagram.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature (2014), the Allen Institute reports a mesoscale mouse connectome: EGFP AAV anterograde tracing, serial two-photon tomography, and informatic registration into a common volume (connectivity.brain-map.org). A computational model addresses strength distributions, symmetry, and network statistics; virtual tractography shows 3D topography. Average correlation 0.90 in 12 duplicate sets supports consistency. Cortico-thalamic pathways exemplify segregation and integration.
summaries.advanced: This is cellular-level mesoscale projection mapping, not EM synaptic resolution—the C. elegans comparison in the abstract is about completeness of a wiring dataset, not matching scale. The matrix can contain false positives (tissue/imaging artifacts, injection tracts). AAV promoter/serotype bias is not excluded. Catalog metadata that tag this record as C. elegans are inconsistent with the paper, which is mouse.
